Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Sumber: https://ambcrypto.com/why-binances-kill-switch-couldnt-stop-hackers-from-draining-6-3b-explained/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes.
  • In a recent development, read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes.
  • There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

It has been revealed that read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

In a recent development, read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

Binance encountered a rather expensive version of that problem on 29th October. Attackers compromised its wallet signing infrastructure and obtained authority to move cryptocurrency through mechanisms that did not depend on the exchange’s ordinary withdrawal process. Suspending withdrawals could interrupt that process. It could do considerably less about permissions already established on Ethereum.

By the time the attack was contained, approximately $6.3 billion had been stolen and Binance’s engineers had developed a specialised procedure to revoke malicious on-chain authority. The exchange could shut down affected services, but Ethereum would continue recognising the delegation until it was explicitly cleared.

Brian Cubellis, Chief Strategy Officer at Bitcoin custody platform Onramp, offered his two cents to AMBCrypto,.

Pausing withdrawals turns off the exchange’s own software, but it does nothing about permissions the attacker has already written to the blockchain.

The distinction is an uncomfortable one for an institution entrusted with billions in customer assets.

It has been revealed that binance subsequently coordinated freezes of stolen funds and began replenishing the affected holdings, reporting approximately 98% replenishment by 4th November. Its financial response was substantial.

However, it still is worth questioning what remained possible while its emergency controls were taking effect.

By the way, for those unaware, the attack began well before 29th October and nowhere near a blockchain.

Sources indicate that according to Binance’s 3rd November incident report, an engineer downloaded a tampered installation package for an AI coding tool in June. The exchange detected the anomaly and replaced the device, but the attackers had already gathered intelligence about its employees and infrastructure. Well into September, another engineer was approached through a fictitious recruitment process involving interviews and a malicious coding assignment.

By 20th October, the attackers had used compromised employee systems and internal AI tooling to access additional machines. In doing so, they ultimately obtained credentials that opened the way to Binance’s wallet signing infrastructure.

In a recent development, it all paid off on the 29th. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, hot wallets transferred approximately 223.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker controlled addresses. Bitcoin and other assets followed. Chainalysis subsequently estimated the overall theft at approximately $6.4 billion.

What was the most consequential part of this intrusion though? The attackers gained access to Binance’s signing infrastructure, the very machinery responsible for authorizing transactions.

On Ethereum, the attackers exploited EIP-7702, a mechanism that allows an externally owned account to delegate execution to smart-contract code.

It has been revealed that ordinarily, that flexibility expands what a wallet can do. Here, according to Binance, the compromised signing infrastructure was used to grant malicious code execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. The exchange described 50 signed transactions involved in manipulating the account’s nonce and establishing the delegation.

Industry observers note that the unsettling part comes next though. Those permissions remained valid on-chain even after Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down its hot-wallet services. The exchange could stop its own systems from processing transactions, but it could not simply switch off the authority the attackers had already established on Ethereum.

It has been revealed that then came another complication. Binance’s hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which distributes the production of cryptographic signatures across multiple participants or components rather than relying on a single conventional private key. That architecture can reduce certain risks, but it also meant there was no single private key available to revoke the malicious delegation immediately.

In a recent development, binance’s engineers had to DEVELOP a specialised revocation procedure while the incident was UNFOLDING. Of course, this took additional time, prolonging the effort to contain unauthorized asset movements.

In a recent development, at 23:56 UTC, the final reported unauthorized Ethereum transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was confirmed on-chain. Binance said it had been broadcast earlier and remained pending before confirmation. At 00:10 UTC on 30th October, the exchange cleared the malicious EIP-7702 delegation with a fresh authorization to the zero address.

Sources indicate that the distinction between broadcast and confirmation matters. So does the absence of an established total for funds transferred after withdrawals were suspended.

Binance acknowledged that suspension alone could not stop every unauthorized movement, but its disclosures do not establish a reconciled post-suspension loss figure.

In a recent development, there is a comforting simplicity to the idea of a kill switch. Something goes wrong, someone pulls the plug and the damage stops. Unfortunately, the blockchain has no particular obligation to respect an exchange’s internal emergency procedures.

Recent findings suggest that consider a hotel discovering that someone has obtained an unauthorized key card. Closing reception prevents new cards from being issued. The existing card still opens the door. Cancelling it, securing the valuables, and recovering what has already disappeared are separate jobs.

Now, this comparison has its limits, but it captures the dilemma facing exchanges whose wallet permissions outlive their own systems.

The problem surfaced in a public exchange between Haseeb Qureshi, Managing Partner at Dragonfly, and  Tudor Anastasiu. Tudor Anastasiu is a blockchain infrastructure and security engineer and the founder of Anastasiu Labs.

The disagreement exposes a distinction that is easy to overlook in the middle of a breach.

According to recent reports, A defensive sweep can move assets to safety, provided the exchange can authorize and execute it before the attacker does. However, moving funds does not necessarily invalidate permissions already granted on-chain and it certainly cannot retrieve assets that have already disappeared.

So, that leaves a rather awkward question: If the signing infrastructure itself has been compromised, how does an exchange authorize an emergency transaction without trusting the very system it suspects?

Carlos Vendrell, Founder of Zealynx Security, sees the answer in testing the procedure under exactly those conditions.

The drill should start from a list of every approval and delegation each hot wallet has given, then revoke one of them for real while assuming the normal signing service is the compromised part, and time it.

Binance’s experience does not establish that MPC inherently prevents rapid revocation. Nor does its disclosure prove that no emergency procedure existed before the breach.

However, it does establish that engineers developed a specialised procedure during the incident and doing so took additional time.

Industry observers note that there was another complication here, one that made the situation look almost absurd. The compromised wallet was reportedly STILL receiving money.

In an analysis dated 4th November, Four Pillars reported that Binance’s deposit-consolidation system continued collecting funds into a compromised Ethereum wallet identified as Binance 14. This allowed the attacker to sweep newly arriving assets.

Nexus Mutual’s reconstruction offers a particularly striking sequence.

At approximately 21:44 UTC, it says the attacker swept 200 million USDT that another Binance-labelled wallet had deposited roughly 72 seconds earlier. Seventy-two seconds! Barely enough time to make a cup of coffee, yet apparently sufficient for a fresh transfer to reach a compromised address and disappear.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers’ findings raise a problem distinct from EIP-7702. An exchange can work to revoke an attacker’s authority while other operational systems continue directing funds towards a dangerous destination. Interrupting those internal asset flows is another containment task and requires its own controls and confirmation.

According to Brian Cubellis, emergency preparedness must account for the loss of the usual signing infrastructure.

An exchange should prove, before it is attacked, that it can cancel any permission on its wallets and move exposed funds to safety even if its own signing system has been taken over.

That is easier prescribed than engineered though.

An independent emergency signing path may accelerate recovery, but it also introduces powerful authority that must be secured. Build too much dependence into the ordinary system and the emergency route may fail alongside it. Concentrate too much authority in the alternative and the supposed safeguard becomes another attractive target.

Once stolen assets leave the exchange’s immediate control, containment becomes a race involving investigators, stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks and the attacker.

Chainalysis’s investigation also described an attempt to move approximately $500 million in stablecoins through a swapping address. Within roughly 20 minutes, the attackers reportedly converted around $325 million into assets less susceptible to issuer freezes, including Ether. The remaining $175 million was frozen.

It has been revealed that there was a reason for the rush. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle can freeze certain tokens at designated addresses. Bitcoin and Ether, by contrast, have no equivalent central issuer with that power. Converting the stolen stablecoins into other assets could therefore put them beyond the reach of an issuer-imposed freeze.

It has been revealed that this whole episode illustrates the limits of intervention once funds have escaped. Investigators may be able to follow the money on-chain, but knowing where it has gone does not necessarily give them the power to retrieve it.

Binance nevertheless managed to secure a substantial portion of the stolen assets. In its 3rd November report, the exchange noted that approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted through cooperation with issuers, law enforcement, and blockchain intelligence firms. By 4th November, it reported replenishing approximately 98% of the affected holdings through replacement purchases.

Industry observers note that of course, Binance had demonstrated considerable capacity to absorb the losses rather than pass them on to people. However, it tells us how much the exchange managed to secure or replace, not how effectively it prevented the attacker from continuing to move assets during the breach.

A year earlier, Bybit had encountered a different version of the problem with compromised transaction authority. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion after compromising the environment associated with its Safe{Wallet} approval process.

Recent findings suggest that according to Bybit’s forensic disclosure, malicious changes deceived signers into approving an unauthorized transaction. It also stated that investigators found no indication that its own infrastructure had been compromised.

Sources indicate that both incidents exposed how much depends on the integrity of the authority behind a transaction. Multiple signatures offer limited protection when signers are misled about what they are approving. And as Binance discovered, shutting down a signing service does not necessarily invalidate authority already established on-chain.

It has been revealed that an emergency kill switch sounds reassuring. Rather less reassuring is discovering, halfway through a breach, that the attacker has permissions your switch cannot revoke.

Binance’s experience raises an uncomfortable question for exchanges entrusted with billions in customer assets — Have they actually tested what happens when the systems responsible for protecting those assets become part of the attack?

An exchange should be able to demonstrate that it can revoke compromised permissions, move exposed assets to safety, and interrupt internal transfers without relying entirely on infrastructure it can no longer trust.

In a recent development, but what should customers make of an exchange’s public assurances when a breach is underway? AMBCrypto put that question to Vik Sharma, Founder and CEO of Cake Wallet,.

A useful update names which approvals were revoked, which assets moved, and where, so customers can check it themselves.

There are legitimate reasons to withhold sensitive operational details while an intrusion is underway. Once the immediate danger has passed, however, an exchange should be able to explain what its emergency controls actually stopped, when compromised authority was extinguished, and whether any assets remained exposed.

Industry observers note that binance deserves credit for publishing details of its response, coordinating substantial asset freezes, and committing its own resources to replenish affected holdings. Those measures helped absorb the financial damage. However, they also revealed why reimbursement and containment should never be confused.

A kill switch should buy defenders control, not merely time to figure out where control has gone.

On 29th October, the largest hack in crypto’s history took Bitcoin to a low near $76,200. A few days later, on 5th November, an AI-driven tech crash spilled into crypto. The Nasdaq 100 fell by 6.4%, while semiconductor stocks tumbled by 12%.

This chaos set off leveraged liquidations of roughly $1.1 billion and pushed Bitcoin’s price below $74,000.

In a recent development, two different shocks, a historical Binance breach, and an AI token sell-off. Though they seem unrelated on the surface, this time they were actually the catalyst for the same event. What Bitcoin saw was a surge in speculative positioning, but what the king coin did not see was a buyer.

According to recent reports, the market’s first take on the Binance hack was that crypto had passed a test. Bitcoin fell by about 6% from its 28th October close — a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns after the controversies surrounding Celsius, FTX, BlockFi, and Bybit.

Matt Mena, Crypto Research Strategist at 21Shares, told AMBCrypto,.

Industry observers note that what we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it. The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, institutional resilience is not retail demand. The market simply treated a smaller slump as evidence of Bitcoin’s underlying strength. However, whether anyone wanted to buy Bitcoin [BTC] was a separate question, one the hack never answered.

Recent findings suggest that still, institutional strength hasn’t eased the feeling of dread felt by many retail investors. And, a major factor can explain why.

Industry observers note that the most important signal is what happened after the liquidations: Nothing. Bitget Wallet’s analysts put it plainly that the leverage reset “has cleared some speculative excess, but is yet to address the underlying demand problem.”.

Looking at the data, one can see why. Most importantly, the ETF flows changed drastically. There were $2.6 billion worth of inflows in September 2026, which turned into $290 million of net outflows in October. Presently, U.S ETF holders sit underwater below their cost basis of $82K.

How ETF holders behave below breakeven remains the key tell for November.

Also, stablecoin supply has not been moving outside the $305 billion zone, a sure sign that liquidity is sitting still.

Finally, one cannot forget the fallout caused by the Binance hack.

According to recent reports, when the exchange reopened withdrawals, the queue moved fast. The exchange processed $4.65 billion against $1.01 billion of deposits in under ten hours; net outflows reached about $5.8 billion over 24 hours!

Each of these factors may not matter when seen separately, but when read together, they describe the same thing — capital leaving or sitting still. The leverage is gone, and the bid is not there to replace it.

For 21Shares, $73,000 is the 200-day moving average, and “the line that would reopen the bear-market debate.”.

Bitget analysts told AMBCrypto that Bitcoin must hold the $73K–$74K range.

The 73,000-74,000 range is now the zone Bitcoin needs to hold. Stabilization would require more balanced derivatives positioning and sustained positive ETF flows. Reclaiming and holding $80,000 would signal stronger demand, while a decisive break below $73,000 could expose $68,000. If $68,000 also fails to hold, the selloff would suggest more than a temporary leverage flush.

When the same number pops up again and again, it stops being a coincidence and starts pointing to a pattern — that Bitcoin is either in a temporary flush or at the start of something deeper.

If buyers do return, Bitcoin can comfortably start holding $80,000, and stronger demand would emerge as a result. Getting back above $81,000 to $82,000 would finally put the largest holder cohorts back in profit.

Recent findings suggest that both reports are similarly aligned on what won’t fix Bitcoin’s buyer problem: Macro relief without demand. In fact, Bitget’s analysts asserted,.

  • South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.
  • On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records.

The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.

On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records. Coinone said it learned about the breach in the same day.

According to Coinone, the information potentially exposed names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, national identification numbers, home and wallet addresses and transaction IDs.

Coinone mentioned the affected data varies by customer, and people who never contacted its support center were unaffected. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

The exchange urged customers who shared passwords during support interactions to change them and warned that fraudsters could impersonate Coinone using details from previous conversations.

Coinone noted its account, trading and wallet infrastructure operates separately from MetaM’s servers, with no evidence of direct compromise. The exchange said it has reported the incident to South Korean authorities.

Industry observers note that the disclosure comes as South Korea moves to strengthen financial-sector cybersecurity. In October, the Financial Services Commission identified security deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial firms reviewed.

On Thursday, the regulator mentioned it would allow crypto exchanges to suspend withdrawals when hacking is suspected, alongside calls for round-the-clock monitoring.

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

In a recent development, dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

According to recent reports, in the speech, Logan remarked the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

In a recent development, her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Recent findings suggest that logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

In a recent development, purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Sources indicate that logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind promptly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

  • The team said that interest accrual on stUSDT ended on Saturday, with holders of stUSDT and its wrapped version, wstUSDT, able to redeem through its official portal until May 14, 2027.

The stUSDT team did not disclose a reason for winding down the RWA protocol but assured holders that all underlying assets remain fully backed.

Real-world asset (RWA) protocol stUSDT has begun winding down operations, nearly three years after reaching a $2.3 billion total value locked (TVL), ending rewards and opening a six-month redemption window for tokenholders.

The team said that interest accrual on stUSDT ended on Saturday, with holders of stUSDT and its wrapped version, wstUSDT, able to redeem through its official portal until May 14, 2027. The team said requests submitted after the deadline will be handled through customer support in monthly batches through August 2027.

The team did not provide a reason for the shutdown but noted all underlying assets remain fully backed. Holders with tokens on exchanges or DeFi platforms must transfer them to personal wallets before redeeming.

Cointelegraph reached out to stUSDT for more information but did not receive a response before publication.

Meanwhile, JustLend DAO mentioned it would phase out supply and borrowing functions for its wstUSDT market as part of the transition.

Released in July 2023 on Tron, stUSDT allowed users to deposit USDT and earn yields from investments in real-world assets, including short-term government bonds. The protocol later expanded to Ethereum.

It has been revealed that according to DefiLlama data, stUSDT’s TVL peaked at about $2.3 billion in November 2023 before declining substantially in subsequent years. It stood at about $8.6 million on Sunday, down from roughly $60 million a year earlier.

Despite its name, stUSDT is not affiliated with stablecoin issuer Tether. In September 2023, Tether denied any affiliation with stUSDT, saying the protocol was an independent project.

It has been revealed that the price of Bitcoin went down from $81,188 on Nov. 4 to $61,956 on Nov. 14, according to CoinGlass data, and the decline amounted to around 24%. On Sunday, Bitcoin recovered to around $65,400.

This week, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared a comparison of Bitcoin charts ahead of the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs and called it "an interesting analysis." Several customers in the replies to his post blamed the drop in Bitcoin on selling by Binance.

Binance is the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, and a large share of futures liquidations takes place on the platform. On Nov. 13, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion in 24 hours, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Still, the CVD on the Binance spot market has stayed positive since Oct. 31.

Coinbase is the custodian for most U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, including BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, and many U.S. institutional investors trade on the platform through Coinbase Prime.

Bitcoin price has plunged toward $65,000, raising fresh concerns about whether BTC could crash toward $60,000. The latest sell-off has pushed Bitcoin below $68,000, while ETF outflows and heavy liquidations continue to weaken market demand. With BTC approaching a critical support zone after several consecutive weekly losses, investors are watching for signs of a reversal. Is Bitcoin heading toward $60K, or can buyers stop the decline?

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin’s breakdown below $68,000 has shifted the market’s attention toward lower support levels. The cryptocurrency dropped below $66,000 on November 14, reaching its weakest level since August as selling pressure continued through the weekend.

The decline has also extended Bitcoin’s losing streak, putting it on course for a sixth consecutive weekly loss. From its October highs near $86,000, BTC has now surrendered a substantial portion of its gains.

Macroeconomic concerns are adding to the pressure. Hotter US inflation has strengthened expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases, while a stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields have reduced appetite for riskier assets. That combination leaves Bitcoin vulnerable as investors reassess their exposure to speculative investments.

Institutional demand is becoming another major concern for Bitcoin investors. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $185.45 million in net outflows on November 13, extending their withdrawal streak to seven consecutive trading sessions.

Sources indicate that the cumulative outflows reached roughly $1.91 billion between November 5 and November 13. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for a significant portion of the withdrawals, highlighting the scale of institutional selling pressure.

It has been revealed that the immediate concern is whether persistent redemptions will continue to weaken demand. If ETF withdrawals extend into another week, Bitcoin could struggle to attract enough buying interest to establish a durable recovery.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s decline has also triggered a major wave of forced selling across the derivatives market. Approximately $1.5 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with bullish positions accounting for the overwhelming majority.

Bitcoin positions represented a substantial share of those liquidations. When leveraged long positions are forcibly closed, exchanges sell the underlying exposure, potentially accelerating an existing decline.

In a recent development, this creates additional pressure during periods of weak liquidity. Traders who expected Bitcoin to recover are being forced out of positions, while fresh buyers remain cautious about entering before the market stabilizes.

Bitcoin price is approaching a critical technical zone after losing the $70,000 and $68,000 levels. The price action highlights a sustained downward trend, with lower highs and lower lows indicating that sellers remain in control.

In a recent development, the $64,000–$68,000 region is now an key demand zone. However, a sustained breakdown below $64,000 would expose the next major support near $60,000–$61,000. That level could become the market’s next significant test if selling pressure continues.

Industry observers note that on the upside, Bitcoin needs to reclaim $70,000 before a stronger recovery can take shape. The $75,000–$77,000 region remains a broader resistance zone that buyers would need to overcome to improve the technical outlook.

AI models agreed more closely with one another than with laboratory measurements in a new test of AI predictions. Pooling their rankings improved results on average, but several systems could still share the same mistake.

In a recent development, the Science Prediction Universe study, led by UniPat AI and submitted to arXiv on Nov. 11, tested 13 agent configurations spanning 12 models on 100 public tasks and 16 private tasks. Each configuration combined a model, reasoning setting and agent software. The study asked them to rank specified experiments across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine.

Science Prediction Universe researchers reported that, on the public tasks, average agreement between scored configurations reached a Spearman rank correlation of 0.52, compared with 0.33 against measured outcomes. Agreement between agents exceeded their correlation with measurements on 81 of the 100 tasks. These averages use available scored predictions, with coverage varying by configuration.

Those figures describe how closely orderings match, rather than percentages of answers correct. Agents might rank reaction conditions by yield or materials by conductivity without having to predict numerical values. A perfect ordering without measurement ties scores 1; random rankings average 0.

The researchers found a benefit to pooling predictions. Averaging each experiment's position across configurations produced a consensus ranking that scored 0.08 points above the average submission, improving results on 73 of the 100 public tasks. The reported 95% confidence interval for the gain was 0.05 to 0.11.

On one oncology task, eleven configurations agreed at 0.9 but averaged just 0.27 against measurements. The benchmark’s best individual system also beat the consensus of its peers on matched tasks.

Sources indicate that more broadly, tasks with greater agreement tended to have better predictions. The paper's agreement analysis therefore presents consensus as an informative but fallible signal. The authors explain that averaging can reduce errors that differ between systems while retaining common ones.

#523. Blockstream And Thales Launch Bitcoin Custody System

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words)

Blockstream And Thales Launch Bitcoin Custody System

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/blockstream-and-thales-launch-bitcoin-custody-system/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest crypto hack in history started with a fake job interview.
  • Sources indicate that blockstream, the tech giant led by co-founder and CEO Adam Back, has debuted an enterprise custody solution developed with French technology and cybersecurity group Thales, according to a company announcement on Nov.
  • The pitch is straightforward: keep the most sensitive part of moving bitcoin, signing transactions, locked inside dedicated security hardware where hackers cannot reach it.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest crypto hack in history started with a fake job interview. Now one of Bitcoin’s oldest infrastructure firms is betting that the answer to AI-era attacks is simpler, hardware-first Bitcoin custody.

Sources indicate that blockstream, the tech giant led by co-founder and CEO Adam Back, has debuted an enterprise custody solution developed with French technology and cybersecurity group Thales, according to a company announcement on Nov. 13.

The pitch is straightforward: keep the most sensitive part of moving bitcoin, signing transactions, locked inside dedicated security hardware where hackers cannot reach it.

And the timing could not be more relevant.

The solution is delivered through Blockstream Enterprise, the company’s institutional platform, and builds on a two-year relationship between the two firms.

Recent findings suggest that it combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation, or Secure-MPC. MPC spreads signing authority across several parties, so no single person or device controls the private key.

The key difference is where that process happens. Blockstream indicates its system executes the signing protocol entirely within the HSM’s secure environment, while conventional MPC solutions may expose parts of the process to general-purpose computers that are easier to attack.

The system also uses FROST, a threshold signing protocol that lets multiple authorized parties jointly produce a signature without ever reconstructing the full private key.

“By moving MPC execution inside the HSM, this architecture addresses critical security risks,” said Jeff Boortz, Blockstream’s chief product officer.

The launch comes just two weeks after hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance, an attack the FBI attributed to North Korea.

Recent findings suggest that the weak point was not the blockchain. It was people and connected computers. Binance said attackers staged fake job interviews and planted malware in a coding assignment downloaded onto an engineer’s work computer.

It has been revealed that AI played a role too. The campaign included a June incident in which a wallet engineer downloaded a tampered installer while looking for an AI coding tool. By Oct. 20, the attackers had used a compromised computer and an internal AI tool to break into the machines of two more employees working on Binance’s wallet infrastructure, according to BleepingComputer, obtaining credentials and a container deployment token.

It has been revealed that that chain of events is exactly what hardware-based Bitcoin custody is designed to stop. If signing keys never leave a sealed device, a hacked laptop is far less useful.

In a recent development, adam Back, the cryptographer whose Hashcash system helped lay the groundwork for Bitcoin’s proof-of-work, has long championed offline key storage. Blockstream already builds hardware wallets and HSMs for cold storage, alongside enterprise wallets for custodians.

Sources indicate that the broader industry is moving in the same direction. Thales has also expanded its work with Fireblocks to keep signing operations inside customer-owned HSMs at banks and regulated institutions.

It has been revealed that the idea is simple. As AI makes it easier for attackers to find small mistakes in complex software, the safest approach is to cut down the number of places where keys can be exposed.

Blockstream knows the stakes firsthand. In September, its Liquid Network sidechain was drained of nearly 4,000 BTC through a software bug, with the attackers returning 3,400 BTC after the flaw was patched.

For institutions, security is the gatekeeper. Banks and asset managers cannot hold bitcoin at scale without custody that meets the same standards as the rest of their operations.

“Financial institutions require secure, reliable infrastructure as they integrate bitcoin into their existing operations,” stated Michael Minkevich, Blockstream’s president and chief operating officer.

Recent findings suggest that that demand has been building since spot Bitcoin ETFs became top performers after their 2024 launch, pulling Wall Street deeper into the asset. Stronger custody options make it easier for the next wave of institutions to follow.

Recent findings suggest that the market itself is under pressure, with Bitcoin trading below $70,000 after a sharp sell-off. But behind the price, the infrastructure that will hold the next trillion dollars of bitcoin keeps getting stronger. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Will the Binance hack push more institutions toward hardware-based Bitcoin custody, or is self-custody in cold storage still the only real answer?

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is sending out a hopeful message to the crypto space in the wake of a brutal market crash that is causing ADA to come very close to falling out of the top 20 crypto assets.

Recently, Hoskinson took to X to respond to a frustrated Cardano fan who posted a screenshot showing ADA falling almost 10% in the last 24 hours.

“It’s all going to be ok,” said Hoskinson. “Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy.”.

The recent crypto market crash has proven to be extremely brutal for a lot of different assets, and Cardano is certainly one of the worst affected.

In recent trading, ADA has fallen all the way down to around $0.15.

At these levels, ADA is currently down around 95% from its all-time high of $3.09, which was reached in September 2021, based on data from CoinGecko.

This represents an almost complete loss of investment value for those who bought at the all-time high.

Overall, Cardano is also down around 35% in the last month and almost 60% since the start of 2026.

As a result, Cardano’s market cap has fallen all the way down to around $5.7 billion, with ADA dropping to 18th place in CoinGecko’s crypto rankings.

This is a very precarious position for the once-dominant altcoin Cardano, which is now extremely close to falling out of the top 20.

It seems as though there are a few different factors at play behind Cardano’s poor performance.

In a recent development, first of all, there has been a huge sell-off in the broader crypto market. Bitcoin has seen major drops, leading to more selling pressure on major altcoins.

This decline has coincided with a falling technology stock market, ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty, outflows from crypto investment products, and mass liquidations of leveraged positions.

That stated, there are clearly some challenges with Cardano beyond the wider market struggles.

Industry observers note that for one, Cardano has faced a lot of criticism over the years for the blockchain’s relatively low adoption, even after years of development. This is especially evident when compared to other chains like Ethereum and Solana.

In fact, Cardano’s decentralized finance ecosystem has recently seen around $46 million in total value locked, as reported by DefiLlama.

Elsewhere, Hoskinson recently found himself embroiled in another controversy surrounding Cardano’s future.

In another recent X post, Hoskinson lashed out at certain commentators who keep bashing the blockchain for its apparent lack of adoption.

He noted that critics initially claimed Cardano suffered from poor on-chain metrics, few real-world use cases and technology that no one wanted to use.

Then, when Hoskinson decided to work on developing apps that would be able to attract millions of people and billions in assets, it seemed as though those same critics began claiming he was scamming everyone.

It has been revealed that “You people are both stupid and scum. I can’t fix stupid,” said Hoskinson. “Grow up.”.

#527. Are Whales Selling Bitcoin For The Anthropic IPO? The SpaceX Playbook Hints A Bottom Is Near

Are Whales Selling Bitcoin For The Anthropic IPO? The SpaceX Playbook Hints A Bottom Is Near

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/are-whales-selling-bitcoin-for-the-anthropic-ipo/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, bitcoin is bleeding ahead of the biggest AI listing in history.
  • BTC dropped below $67,000 this week, its weakest level since August, as investors pulled money from spot ETFs ahead of the Anthropic IPO.
  • In a recent development, the massive question on crypto is simple: are whales selling bitcoin to buy into the Anthropic IPO?

According to recent reports, bitcoin is bleeding ahead of the biggest AI listing in history. But if the market follows the script it wrote just five months ago, the selling could soon run out of fuel.

BTC dropped below $67,000 this week, its weakest level since August, as investors pulled money from spot ETFs ahead of the Anthropic IPO. Anthropic is set to price its shares on Nov. 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19.

In a recent development, the massive question on crypto is simple: are whales selling bitcoin to buy into the Anthropic IPO? The data offers some clues.

Sources indicate that according to figures circulating widely on X, about $2.35 billion has flowed out of US spot Bitcoin ETFs over the past two weeks. BlackRock’s IBIT has led the exodus with 11 straight sessions of redemptions, accounting for roughly 90% of November’s outflows.

Macro pressure is adding to the strain. Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s support for a December rate hike pushed CME FedWatch odds of such a move to 96.3%, while a tech sell-off has weighed on all risk assets. Bitcoin crashed below $70,000 earlier this week as liquidations topped $1.6 billion.

This has happened before. In the run-up to SpaceX’s record $75 billion IPO in June, Bitcoin went through an almost identical cycle:.

The bottom is well documented. Bitcoin touched as low as $59,375 on June 5, as data showed at the time. Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick then called the cycle low, arguing that heavy selling of spot Bitcoin ETFs, partly to free cash for SpaceX’s IPO, was likely to ease once the listing began.

Sources indicate that the scale of that drain was large. More than $5.72 billion of spot Bitcoin ETF redemptions since mid-May were tied to investors freeing capital for the SpaceX offering.

It has been revealed that crypto analyst Benjamin Cowen took the comparison a step further. In a post on X, e overlaid Bitcoin’s price in the 30 days before and after the SpaceX IPO with its performance in the roughly 30 days leading up to the Anthropic listing.

The two lines move almost in lockstep through the start of the window, each slipping a few percent in the first week.

The SpaceX path also offers a lesson in patience. In Cowen’s chart, Bitcoin was down about 20% by SpaceX’s listing day and dipped to roughly 25% below its starting point in the weeks after, before stabilizing. The real recovery came later, once the IPO selling pressure had fully cleared.

In a recent development, if the pattern holds, more selling could happen around Nov. 19. But it would also suggest the market is in the late stages of the drawdown, not the beginning.

There are two reasons the selling pressure could be lighter this time.

First, the retail slice is smaller. Anthropic expects to allocate up to 20% of its IPO shares to retail investors, about $11.55 billion to $12.87 billion at its price range, according to FourWeekMBA’s analysis of the organization’s amended prospectus. SpaceX initially planned to give retail around 30% of a much larger $75 billion deal, before trimming it to the low 20% range.

A smaller retail pool means less cash that needs to be raised, potentially by selling crypto.

Recent findings suggest that second, Anthropic’s separate $26 billion private placement is being funded by its own compute suppliers, including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft. That money comes from corporate balance sheets, not the same pool of investor cash that might otherwise sit in bitcoin.

The first level for bulls is $70,000. Reclaiming it would show buyers stepping back in after a sharp week.

Above that, the $76,000 zone is the next key hurdle, followed by the $80,000 to $82,000 resistance range.

According to recent reports, on the downside, this week’s low near $67,000 is the line to hold. A break below it could open a move toward the $59,000 to $60,000 area, the same zone where Bitcoin bottomed before the SpaceX listing.

According to recent reports, still, the IPO is not the only driver. If the Fed’s rate decision and the tech sell-off keep pushing investors out of risk, the end of IPO selling alone won’t be enough to turn Bitcoin around. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Tech Report: Newly introduced Monero Privacy Update Might Be Coming Soon: Key Improvement

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://u.today/new-monero-privacy-update-might-be-coming-soon-key-improvement

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.
  • The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is right now pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The glitch lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

At the moment, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

It has been revealed that while the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

Sources indicate that once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Presently, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

Over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for users that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

Sources indicate that when the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

Solana’s biggest week of the year got off to a painful start. But beneath the price chart, Solana staking tells a very different story.

It has been revealed that SOL fell as low as $67.37 overnight into Sunday, its lowest level since late June. The drop landed on the very first day of Breakpoint, the Solana Foundation’s flagship conference, held in London for the first time from Nov. 15 to 17.

Sources indicate that the token is now trading near $70, down about 6.8% in 24 hours and more than 20% below where it stood on Nov. 4.

Yet roughly two-thirds of all SOL remains locked up in staking, and holders show little sign of rushing for the exits.

It has been revealed that the sell-off has little to do with Solana itself. It is being driven by the same macro pressure hitting the entire crypto market.

Industry observers note that fed Governor Christopher Waller’s support for a December rate hike pushed CME FedWatch odds of such a move to 96.3%, per BigGo Finance. The crypto Fear and Greed Index has sunk to 13, deep in extreme fear territory, while Bitcoin has dropped below $70,000.

Institutional demand has also cooled. US spot Solana ETFs have now posted seven straight days of outflows totaling around $58.3 million, a sharp contrast to earlier this year, when Solana ETF inflows topped $1.16 billion.

Recent findings suggest that leverage did the rest. Around $67 million in long positions were liquidated as SOL broke through support, forcing more selling into a falling market.

Here is where the picture changes. As of Nov. 8, 434.15 million SOL was staked with voting validators, or 68.14% of the total supply, according to Cryptoticker’s analysis.

Recent findings suggest that bitwise’s latest staking report found that Solana ended the third quarter with 69% of its supply staked, the highest of the six networks it tracks. By comparison, Ethereum stood at 33%.

On Solana, staking has become the default. Holding unstaked SOL is the exception, not the rule.

According to recent reports, stakers are earning a gross yield of about 5.2%, or close to 5% after a typical validator commission. High participation strengthens network security and keeps a large share of supply off the market, which helps limit the pool of coins available to sell during panics like this one.

The ratio has slipped slightly in recent weeks, with around 4.8 million SOL leaving active staking over 30 days. But with nearly 70% of supply still committed, the core holder base remains firmly in place.

The timing of the crash is awkward, but it also puts the spotlight on what comes next. More than 8,000 attendees are expected at London’s Olympia this week, with sessions focused on stablecoins, onchain capital markets and AI agents.

Development has not slowed down either. Arcium recently opened Blackthorn, a private AI inference stack built for Solana that runs AI models with prompts, outputs and model weights encrypted. That builds on October’s Alpenglow upgrade, which cut finality to around 150 milliseconds.

It has been revealed that past conferences show the price reaction can vary. At Breakpoint 2023 in Amsterdam, SOL rallied 20% during the event and kept climbing for weeks. In Abu Dhabi last year, the price slipped 2.3% during the conference before recovering over the following month.

According to recent reports, the first line to hold is the overnight low near $67.40. Holding above it would suggest sellers are running out of steam after a brutal week.

Industry observers note that on the upside, SOL needs to reclaim the August level around $71.90 first, then the $75 to $80 zone it lost over the past two days. A move back above $80 would put SOL back in the range it held before its earlier slide below that level.

The bigger target is the 200-day moving average, just under $89. Reclaiming that line would mark a clear trend shift.

If $67 fails, the psychological $60 level becomes the next major support.

For now, Solana staking data reveals that most holders are choosing to stay put and earn yield rather than sell into the panic. For more updates, follow the latest altcoin news.

Can Breakpoint spark a SOL recovery this week, or does the price need to retest $60 before Solana’s strong staking base pays off?

#534. Breaking: AI Cyberattacks And Outages Keep Breaking Centralized Systems, But Bitcoin Keeps Running

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words)
AI & Tech

Breaking: AI Cyberattacks And Outages Keep Breaking Centralized Systems, But Bitcoin Keeps Running

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/ai-cyberattacks-outages-keep-breaking-centralized-systems-but-bitcoin-keeps-running/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AI cyberattacks and outages have made the past few months brutal for the systems the modern internet runs on.
  • Yet through all of it, one network never missed a beat.
  • Sources indicate that the Bitcoin blockchain has been running continuously since 2009 and has never been breached.

According to recent reports, AI cyberattacks and outages have made the past few months brutal for the systems the modern internet runs on. Cloud platforms have gone dark, AI tools have failed in waves, and hackers have pulled off the biggest heist in history.

Yet through all of it, one network never missed a beat.

Sources indicate that the Bitcoin blockchain has been running continuously since 2009 and has never been breached. As AI makes attacks faster and outages more disruptive, that track record is becoming one of crypto’s strongest selling points.

It has been revealed that the latest disruption started on Nov. 12, when a Microsoft outage centered on Exchange Online knocked out Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot. By its second day, it had also broken the Microsoft 365 connectors inside ChatGPT and Claude, cutting both AI assistants off from owners’ work email, calendars and documents.

On Nov. 13, Anthropic also opened a separate incident as consumers struggled to log in to Claude.ai and Claude Code. Neither organization has linked the problems to an attack.

It has been revealed that it was not the first time. On Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok went down at roughly the same time. xAI blamed an outage at its Memphis data center, but the timing set off speculation. Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson suggested a nation state may have been behind it, a theory that remains unconfirmed.

The outages came alongside a wave of real attacks. Security firm Wiz dubbed last month “Black October” after counting at least nine AI development platforms that disclosed security incidents.

According to recent reports, many of those attacks aimed to steal API keys for AI models, and in some cases researchers suspected AI “agent swarms” were doing the work. AI is now both a target and a weapon.

Crypto has already felt the impact. In August, Bitcoin swap protocol Boltz suspended its services after attackers used AI to probe and exploit vulnerabilities faster than the team could patch them.

Coinbase’s chief security officer Philip Martin has warned that advanced AI models “will accelerate digital threats as well as digital defense.”.

Then came the biggest one of all. On Oct. 29, hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance’s hot wallets, the largest crypto theft on record. The FBI attributed it to North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit, the same group behind the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025.

Investigators traced the entry point to a compromised employee laptop. In other words, the weak spot was a centralized company’s internal systems, not the blockchains themselves.

Industry observers note that the response highlighted the industry’s resilience. Binance stated it replenished around 90% of the stolen assets within days, and stablecoin issuers froze more than $2.4 billion of the stolen funds.

Notably, when Binance began reopening withdrawals, the first network it switched back on was Bitcoin.

Recent findings suggest that there is a clear pattern here. Every major failure, from Microsoft’s cloud to AI chatbots to Binance’s hot wallets, happened at a single point of control. When that one point breaks, everything built on it goes down.

Sources indicate that bitcoin is built the opposite way. Thousands of independent nodes around the world keep the network running, so there is no single server to take offline and no single company to hack.

That is why every substantial outage revives the case for decentralized infrastructure. It is also why the network is finding latest roles in the AI economy. Lightning Labs just released payments for autonomous AI agents, letting software pay for computing directly in bitcoin.

According to recent reports, the lesson for investors is straightforward. The risk lives at the edges: exchanges, custodians, wallets and the cloud services they rely on. Holding coins in self-custody and choosing platforms with strong security practices matter more than ever in an age of AI-powered attacks.

Sources indicate that the hacks have weighed on sentiment. Bitcoin fell nearly 5% after the Binance theft, and it has since dropped below $70,000 amid a broader risk-off move.

But the network itself has not wavered. Blocks keep coming, transactions keep settling, and the protocol keeps working, whether ChatGPT is online or not. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Will AI-powered cyberattacks push more people toward decentralized networks like Bitcoin, or will they make crypto platforms an even bigger target?
